newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Differences over Security Council draft on Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Differences over Security Council draft on Cyprus.

text.p: The United States had wanted a Security Council resolution due to be adopted on Monday to mention the purchase by Cyprus of Russian-made tanks and missiles, but this was softened to a reference to "sophisticated weaponry," sources at the United Nations said on Saturday.
The Cyprus delegation, representing the internationally recognised Greek Cypriot-led government in Nicosia, was also said to be unhappy over some of the draft's language.

The resolution will renew the mandate of the 1,200-member U.N. force stationed on the island since 1964 and also support efforts for a new major effort in the new year to resolve the long-running Cyprus question.

The island has been virtually partitioned into a Greek Cypriot south and a Turkish Cypriot north since troops from Turkey landed in 1974 in response to a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece.
The planned resolution echoes oft-repeated fears, expressed again in a recent report by Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, that both parts of the island have become dangerously militarized.

The sources at the United Nations said the United States had wanted a specific reference to the Cyprus government's purchase of tanks, which include T-80UM main battle tanks from Russia, and its intention to acquire Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles.

But after objections mainly by Russia during consultations among the five permanent members of the Security Council, this was changed to a renewed expression of concern about excessive levels of military forces and armaments and the rate at which they were being expanded, upgraded and modernised, "including by the introduction of sophisticated weaponry," without specifically mentioning tanks or missiles.

The same paragraph in the draft also expresses concern about the "lack of progress towards a significant reduction in the number of foreign troops" in Cyprus, where the United Nations says Turkey still maintains a force of about 30,000.
The sources also said the Cyprus U.N. delegation had reservations about the political implications of some of the draft's language.

They referred particularly to a paragraph emphasising the responsibility of the "authorities of both communities to maintain law and order, "after several violent incidents in recent months in which three Greek Cypriot civilians and a Turkish Cypriot soldier were killed.

The government regards law and order as a matter of state responsibility and objects to being put on a par with the Turkish Cypriot community, which proclaimed its own breakaway state in 1983 that is recognised only by Turkey.
